variants.name: async fn + .await on a runtime (tokio/async-std)
variants.idiom_name: async fn returning impl Future, driven with .await and spawned tasks
variants.implementation_notes: Rust's language form is async/await: an async fn desugars to a function returning a value that implements std::future::Future, and .await drives it - poll attempts to resolve the future and, when it cannot, registers a Waker instead of blocking the thread. The standard library supplies the trait and the task plumbing but no executor, so a runtime crate (tokio, async-std, smol) drives tasks and provides spawn and task handles for fan-out; futures are lazy, so nothing runs until it is awaited or spawned.
variants.code_sketch:
async fn load(id: u64) -> Summary {          // async fn: a future
    fetch(id).await                              // .await suspends, not blocks
}

let pending = tokio::spawn(load(1));              // task handle: pending value
let summary = pending.await?;                     // read end, resumed by the Waker
let out = futures::executor::block_on(load(2));   // only outside async contexts
pitfalls: Futures are lazy: an unawaited or dropped future never runs at all, so work that must happen has to be spawned and its task handle kept (dropping the handle detaches the task).

Blocking calls (std::thread::sleep, synchronous I/O, CPU loops) stall a runtime worker, and holding a non-Send borrow across .await makes the future unspawnable on a multithreaded runtime - use spawn_blocking for blocking work.
Cancellation is drop-based: dropping a future stops it only at the next await point, and a spawned task needs an explicit abort handle to be stopped at all.

variants.name: futures-crate combinator style driven by an executor
variants.implementation_notes: The combinator style builds pending values without async syntax: the futures crate composes futures as values (map, and_then, join, try_join) and an executor - block_on or futures::executor - drives them to completion, which is also how the crate documents its task system. It fits library code that must not assume a runtime and dynamic fan-in where join_all or select_all over a collection reads better than a macro; the async/await variant remains the default in application code.
pitfalls: Combinator chains hide where the continuation runs (whichever executor polls), and mixing them with .await in one function produces confusing Send-inference errors.
Without an executor a composed future does nothing at all, and calling block_on from inside an async context is a deadlock rather than a wait.

variants.name: std thread + mpsc channel (no runtime)
variants.implementation_notes: The std-only realization predates async Rust: spawn a thread for the work, send the outcome down a channel (or return it through the thread's join handle), and let the consumer receive it - the Sender is the write end and the Receiver the read end, with recv() blocking and try_recv() polling. Use it when the operation is genuinely blocking (FFI, filesystem, a library without async support) or when the program has no runtime and one thread per pending value is affordable.
pitfalls: recv() blocks forever when the producer panics or returns early without sending: send on every exit path, or treat a RecvError (disconnected channel) as the failure signal.
One receiver is the single consumer by construction - sharing it across threads needs a Mutex, and several pending values multiplexed over one channel need a tag or reply channel per request.
